dataset.name: Soil carbon, nitrogen, and ice content data (2014-2018) at Happy Valley and Sagwon Hills in Northern Alaska, United States
description: This dataset contains three data files from soil data collected by sampling soil cores and pits across a toposequence on two hillslopes in permafrost affected soils in Northern Alaska, USA. Soil cores and profiles were excavated to 3m or until auger refusal. Samples were collected by genetic soil horizons for laboratory analysis and organized into complete soil profiles ordered depth. Soil carbon, nitrogen, and ice stocks (stocks_by_core.csv) were calculated from the core dataset . Data for mean values by depth increments (20,50,100,150,200 cm) of total soc, total nitrogen, bulk density, and ice content were determined and made available in this dataset (soc-tn-bd-ice-slab_tables.csv). Stocks by site are included in a separate file (stocks_by_site.csv). Each of these three files also has an associated data dictionary file (stocks_by_core_dd.csv, soc-tn-bd-ice-slab_tables_dd.csv, stocks_by_site_dd.csv). Finally, an FLMD file is also included (FLMD_Happy_Valley_Sagwon.csv).

measurementTechnique:
Soil morphological characterization and sampling
Sampling occurred in mid-July of 2014 and 2016 (Happy Valley), and 2018 (Sagwon). Sampling locations along each hillslope were chosen to represent major categorical hillslope positions (Summit, Shoulder, Upper and Lower Backslope, Footslope, Toeslope, Basin) (Figure 1). The sampled locations along each hillslope were characterized by northeast to northwest aspects (295° to 51° true north).
At each categorical hillslope position, where drainage allowed, 2 m x 1 m soil pits were dug to a depth of at least 100 cm using a combination of hand tools (for unfrozen active layer excavation) and a gas-powered jackhammer (for excavation into the frozen portion of the active layer and permafrost) following standard procedures for permafrost-affected soils (Ping et al., 2013). These soil pits also enabled two-dimensional characterization of soil variability through scale drawings completed in the field. For sampling locations where the water table did not allow full soil pits to be dug, trenches ~2 m x 60 cm in dimension were excavated with hand tools to the thaw depth at the time of sampling. Sampling of frozen material below the thaw depth was then accomplished through the use of a SIPRE (US Snow, Ice and Permafrost Research Establishment) core auger (Rand and Mellor, 1985) approximately every 50cm along the width of the active layer trench. Therefore, depending on the depth of thaw, a combination of the soil pit and a core or set of cores was utilized to observe material to at least 100 cm in depth at each of the sites and additional coring was conducted at the bottom of each soil pit to make observations to the deepest possible depths. Coring continued until SIPRE auger refusal or cores were unable to be retrieved. Because the lower parent material at both locations was glacial till, coarse fragments were encountered which often limited SIPRE coring depths to less than 300 cm, particularly at upper hillslope positions.
Soil morphology was described in the field, and morphological properties including soil color, soil structure, soil texture, visible secondary carbonates, and visual estimates of coarse fragment volume were utilized to define genetic horizons using USDA-NRCS standardized terminology for horizon nomenclature and soil morphological properties (Schoeneberger et al., 2012). Representative physical samples from each genetic horizon Morphological evidence was utilized to estimate the depth to the bottom of the transient layer – the uppermost portion of the transition zone (transient layer plus the intermediate layer) – which is the portion of the upper permafrost that may join the active layer over decadal timescales due to environmental fluctuations (Shur et al., 2005; French and Shur, 2010). This was considered the permafrost table for the purposes of soil description and was estimated by the first appearance of ice-rich materials which are characteristic of the bottom of the transient layer, such as suspended (ataxitic) cryostructures (Murton and French, 1994, Kanevskiy et al., 2008) and/or ice layers (e.g. lenses or belts) (Shur, 1988, Murton and French, 1994, French and Shur, 2010, Kanevskiy et al., 2011, Murton, 2013). Based on soil morphology and depth to permafrost observations, all sampled soils were classified as Gelisols (Turbels and Histels, U.S. Soil Taxonomy; Soil Survey Staff, 2014) or Cryosols (Turbic and Histic, WRB; IUSS Working Group WRB, 2022).
Two-dimensional field drawings of soil profiles indicating the distribution, to scale, of soil genetic horizons for locations at Happy Valley and Sagwon were digitized into a raster data format using QGIS long term release v3.16 (QGIS Team, 2020). In order to synthesize both soil pit and core data, multiple “pseudocores” were generated from digitized pit drawings to emulate the spatial distribution of SIPRE cores at locations where pits could not be dug. We randomly sampled 10 cm wide increments (approximately the width of the SIPRE core) for every 50 cm of pit width, in order to approximate the spatial distribution of cores taken in positions sampled with active layer trenches and cores only. In cases where core samples were taken from the bottom of a soil pit, pseudocores were centered on the horizontal position of the sampled core. The resulting 51 pseudocore observations were then merged with 39 core observations collected with the SIPRE auger to give a total of 90 observations from both Happy Valley (n=48) and Sagwon (n=42). The depth of these observations ranged from 42 to 304 cm, with an average depth of observation of 137 55 cm.
A total of 615 samples were collected in the field for laboratory analysis from both soil pits and soil cores. Multiple samples were taken from some large genetic horizons, analyzed independently, and later averaged to produce unique values for each genetic horizon. Bulk density samples were collected using standardized methodologies, depending on thermal state and material type (Ping et al., 2013). Surface organic horizon bulk density samples were collected using a serrated knife to cut regular blocks of material. The dimensions of these blocks were measured in the field. For unfrozen mineral horizons, bulk density samples were collected from the pit face using either rings of known volume with sharp beveled edges or cut blocks. Frozen materials exposed in the faces of soil pits were collected using a hole saw attached to a battery-powered hammer drill. The dimensions of samples collected using the hole saw were measured and recorded to calculate volume. Frozen materials extracted by SIPRE corer (7.6 cm inner diameter) were segmented using a knife and a mallet following description of the core, and dimensions were recorded. All samples were immediately sealed in plastic bags to prevent water loss and placed in coolers in the field to minimize thawing of frozen soils. At the end of each day, samples were placed in cold storage at -20°C at Toolik Lake Field Station, AK. Samples were subsequently shipped overnight in a frozen state to Argonne National Laboratory (Lemont, IL), using a 24-hr cargo service from Prudhoe Bay, AK. Upon arrival at Argonne, samples were placed in long-term cold storage at -20°C until they were removed for preparation.

Sample preparation, bulk density and water content determinations
Samples were weighed in a frozen state, thawed overnight at room temperature, and subsequently dried at 60°C. Samples were subsequently hand pulverized and sieved to separate the fine earth (< 2 mm) from live roots (when present) and coarse fragments (> 2 mm). Any coarse fragments and roots collected from each sample were oven dried for 24 hr at 105 ºC, and weighed. Fresh root volume was estimated by assuming fresh weights were double that of dry weights and the density of fresh roots was using an average fresh root density value of approximately 1 g cm-3 (Birouste et al. 2014). A fine-earth (< 2 mm material) subsample was weighed, dried for 24 hr at 105 ºC, and weighed again to obtain a moisture correction factor for determining the oven-dry weight of the bulk fine-earth fraction of each sample. Thus, the bulk densities and all other proportions of soil constituents reported in the data represent percentages of fine-earth material. Coarse fragment free proportions (CFF) of soil were subsequently derived for each sample for use in carbon and ice stock calculations (section 2.6 below).
The gravimetric water content of each sample at the time of collection was determined by the difference between the field-moist mass of the bulk sample and the oven-dry mass of the bulk sample (obtained by applying a moisture correction to the bulk mass of the samples after drying a subsample at 105ºC for 24 hr) and expressed on a dry weight basis. Bulk density was subsequently determined as the oven-dry sample mass by volume, where volume was determined from sample dimensions as described in section 2.2.
Volumetric ice content (Theta-v,i) [m3 ice m3 soil-1] was then determined for samples frozen at the time of sampling as Equation (1), Volumetric ice content = (Gravimetric Water Content x Bulk Density) / Particle Density, where Theta-g is gravimetric water content [kg H2O kg soil-1], Roe-s is the soil bulk density [kg soil m3 soil-1], and Roe-i is the density of ice, taken as 917 kg m-3, Weast, 1981).

Soil chemical characterization
The fine earth fraction was used for all chemical characterizations. Aliquots of each sample were homogenized and ground to a fine powder in a high energy ball mill (Spex SamplePrep 8000D Mixer/Mill, Metuchen, New Jersey) for 2 min., oven dried overnight at 65 °C, and analyzed for total TC and TN by dry combustion at 900 °C with an elemental analyzer (vario MAX cube; Elementar Americas, Inc., Ronkonkoma, New York). Total SOC concentration was determined with the same analyzer at 650 °C (Provin, 2014). Inorganic carbon (IC) concentration was determined by difference (TC − SOC). Soil carbon to nitrogen (C:N) ratios were calculated from SOC and TN data. Soil pH for mineral samples was determined in a 1:1 slurry of 5 g of soil and 5 ml of de-ionized water (Soil Survey Staff, 2014, Soil Survey Staff, 2022). For organic soil samples (> 18% SOC), a 1:2 soil-water slurry was utilized because a 1:1 slurry for organics did not typically produce enough free water to yield a reliable slurry and pH measurement.
